claim: T238 in β-tubulin is solvent inaccessible and resides on helix H7.
source: T238 is solvent inaccessible and resides on a helix (H7) that undergoes a piston-like movement between the two conformations.
evidence: Stated in Figure 1A caption and shown in structural visualization

claim: Helix H7 undergoes a piston-like movement between curved and straight conformations of β-tubulin.
source: T238 is solvent inaccessible and resides on a helix (H7) that undergoes a piston-like movement between the two conformations.
evidence: Stated in text and shown in structural superposition in Figure 1A

claim: Cells expressing T238A αβ-tubulin make longer, less dynamic microtubules than wild-type.
source: Time-lapse imaging of live yeast shows that cells expressing T238A αβ-tubulin make longer, less dynamic microtubules than their wild-type (WT) counterparts.
evidence: Demonstrated by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 1B and Videos 1,2

claim: β:T238A microtubules have normal structure as observed by negative stain electron microscopy.
source: Mutant microtubules have normal structure.
evidence: Shown in electron micrographs in Figure 1C

claim: T238A and wild-type microtubules show similar concentration-dependent growth rates.
source: In vitro, T238A and wild-type microtubules show similar concentration-dependent growth rates (slopes: 29.6 +/- 1.8 µm/hr/µM for wild-type, 25.5 +/- 0.8 µm/hr/µM for β:T238A, the differences between the slopes are not statistically significant
evidence: Quantified from in vitro dynamics measurements shown in Figure 1D

claim: The x-intercepts of elongation rate plots differ between wild-type (0.12 µM) and β:T238A (0.033 µM) by a factor of approximately 3.5, and this difference is statistically significant.
source: x-intercepts: 0.12 µM for wild-type, 0.033 µM for β:T238A, this difference is statistically significant
evidence: Calculated from regression analysis of data in Figure 1D

claim: T238A microtubules catastrophe less frequently than wild-type.
source: T238A microtubules catastrophe less frequently than wild-type (top; N = 99, 115 for wild-type and T238A respectively, bars show s.d.)
evidence: Quantified from in vitro dynamics measurements shown in Figure 1E

claim: β:T238A microtubules shrink approximately hundredfold more slowly than wild-type (1.1 µm/min for β:T238A compared to 96 µm/min for wild-type).
source: after catastrophe β:T238A microtubules shrink roughly hundredfold more slowly than wild-type (1.1 µm/min for β:T238A compared to 96 µm/min for wild-type, Figure 1E, bottom).
evidence: Quantified from in vitro dynamics measurements shown in Figure 1E

claim: The β:T238A mutation significantly strengthens the lattice contacts that dictate the rate of microtubule shrinking.
source: Thus, the mutation significantly strengthens the lattice contacts that dictate the rate of microtubule shrinking.
evidence: Inferred from the hundredfold slower shrinking rate of mutant microtubules

claim: Even in the presence of GTPγS, wild-type microtubules show substantially less nucleation than T238A microtubules.
source: We observed that even in the presence of GTPγS, wild-type microtubules show substantially less nucleation than T238A microtubules (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by fluorescence imaging and spindown assays in Figure 2A,B

claim: The abundant nucleation from the β:T238A mutant cannot be ascribed to a defect in GTPase activity.
source: Thus, the abundant nucleation from the mutant cannot be ascribed to a defect in GTPase activity.
evidence: Concluded from GTPγS nucleation experiments showing differential nucleation persists even when GTP hydrolysis cannot occur

claim: GMPCPP did not support elongation of yeast microtubules in dynamics assays.
source: We initially attempted to use GMPCPP, the hydrolysis-resistant nucleotide of choice for vertebrate microtubules (Hyman et al., 1992), but GMPCPP did not support elongation of yeast microtubules in our dynamics assays.
evidence: Observed experimentally in dynamics assays

claim: GTPγS better mimics GTP for yeast microtubules than GMPCPP.
source: Yeast microtubules polymerized readily in the presence of GTPγS, however, indicating that GTPγS better mimics GTP for yeast microtubules.
evidence: Observed from polymerization experiments comparing GMPCPP and GTPγS

claim: Wild-type and β:T238A microtubules contain similarly low amounts of GTP (2–4% of total exchangeable nucleotide) when assembled with GTPγS.
source: These experiments revealed that wild-type and mutant microtubules contain similarly low amounts of GTP (2–4% of total exchangeable nucleotide) and Pi (fewer than 3% of exchangeable sites) (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: Measured by TLC analysis shown in Figure 2C,D

claim: Wild-type and β:T238A microtubules contain similarly low amounts of Pi (fewer than 3% of exchangeable sites) when assembled with GTPγS.
source: These experiments revealed that wild-type and mutant microtubules contain similarly low amounts of GTP (2–4% of total exchangeable nucleotide) and Pi (fewer than 3% of exchangeable sites) (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: Measured by TLC analysis shown in Figure 2C,D

claim: β:T238A αβ-tubulin remains competent to hydrolyze GTP.
source: these experiments demonstrate that β:T238A αβ-tubulin remains competent to hydrolyze GTP
evidence: Demonstrated by TLC analysis showing GDP in mutant microtubules

claim: The altered nucleation and shrinking behavior of β:T238A cannot be ascribed to an accumulation of GTP or GDP.Pi.
source: the altered nucleation and shrinking behavior cannot be ascribed to an accumulation of GTP or GDP.Pi that might result from a defect in assembly-dependent GTPase activity or phosphate release.
evidence: Concluded from TLC data showing no accumulation of GTP or GDP.Pi in mutant microtubules

claim: Some nonenzymatic mechanism must account for the observed changes in polymerization dynamics caused by the β:T238A mutation.
source: Some other, nonenzymatic mechanism must therefore account for the observed changes in polymerization dynamics.
evidence: Inferred from ruling out GTPase defects as the cause

claim: TOG domains bind tightly to curved αβ-tubulin but very weakly to straight αβ-tubulin.
source: The rationale for this approach is based on the fact that TOG domains bind tightly to curved αβ-tubulin but very weakly to straight (Figure 3A) (Ayaz et al., 2012; 2014 ).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work and illustrated in Figure 3A

claim: TOG1 and TOG2 show very similar affinity (within a factor of two) for unpolymerized T238A αβ-tubulin as they do for wild-type.
source: TOG1 and TOG2, two different TOG domains from the yeast microtubule regulatory factor Stu2p (Wang and Huffaker, 1997), show very similar affinity (within a factor of two) for unpolymerized T238A αβ-tubulin as they do for wild-type (Figure 3B).
evidence: Measured by analytical ultracentrifugation shown in Figure 3B

claim: The β:T238A mutation does not significantly change the conformation of unpolymerized αβ-tubulin.
source: Thus, we conclude that the β:T238A mutation does not significantly change the conformation of unpolymerized αβ-tubulin.
evidence: Concluded from TOG binding data showing similar affinities for wild-type and mutant tubulin

claim: Recent cryo-EM studies provided atomic models for distinct microtubule lattices containing GTP, GTPγS, or GDP, with GTP favoring an 'expanded' form and GTPγS and GDP favoring a 'compacted' form.
source: Recent cryo-EM studies of microtubule structure provided atomic models for distinct microtubule lattices containing GTP, GTPγS, or GDP, with GTP favoring an 'expanded' form and GTPγS and GDP favoring a 'compacted' form (Alushin et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from prior cryo-EM structural studies

claim: Plus-end tracking proteins in the EB1 family discriminate between GTP-like and GDP-like lattices.
source: Plus-end tracking proteins in the EB1 family have been shown to discriminate between these GTP-like and GDP-like lattices (Maurer et al., 2011; 2012; 2014; Zanic et al., 2009).
evidence: Cited from prior studies of EB1 proteins

claim: Bim1-GFP tracks the growing end of yeast microtubules.
source: Control experiments revealed that a Bim1-GFP fusion protein tracked the growing end of yeast microtubules
evidence: Observed in control experiments

claim: Bim1-GFP coats the entire length of GTPγS-containing yeast microtubules with cap-like intensity.
source: Bim1-GFP coated the entire length of GTPγS-containing yeast microtubules with cap-like intensity (Figure 4).
evidence: Observed in fluorescence microscopy experiments shown in Figure 4

claim: Like other EB1 proteins on vertebrate microtubules, Bim1 discriminates between GTP and GDP forms of the yeast microtubule lattice.
source: We therefore infer that like other EB1 proteins on vertebrate microtubules (Zanic et al., 2009; Maurer et al., 2011), Bim1 discriminates between GTP and GDP forms of the yeast microtubule lattice (presumably, expanded and compacted).
evidence: Inferred from Bim1 behavior on GTPγS microtubules and comparison to vertebrate EB1 proteins

claim: At 50 nM concentration, Bim1-GFP coats the entire length of 'dynamic' β:T238A microtubules with cap-like intensity.
source: In marked contrast to its behavior on wild-type microtubules, at 50 nM concentration Bim1-GFP coated the entire length of 'dynamic' β:T238A microtubules with cap-like intensity.
evidence: Observed in fluorescence microscopy experiments shown in Figure 4B

claim: At 5 nM concentration, the Bim1-GFP coat on the body of β:T238A microtubules is slightly weaker than at the cap but still substantially more intense than on wild-type.
source: At lower concentrations (5 nM), the Bim1-GFP coat on the body of β:T238A microtubules is slightly weaker than at the cap but still substantially more intense than on wild-type (Figure 4B).
evidence: Observed in fluorescence microscopy experiments shown in Figure 4B

claim: The β:T238A mutation attenuates the conformational response to GTP hydrolysis in the microtubule lattice.
source: Thus, the β:T238A mutation attenuates the conformational response to GTP hydrolysis in the microtubule lattice.
evidence: Concluded from Bim1 binding data showing GTP-like binding to GDP-containing mutant microtubules

claim: The structural consequence of the β:T238A mutation resembles the effect of taxol binding, which also promotes an expanded conformation of αβ-tubulin in a GDP lattice.
source: The structural consequence of the mutation resembles the effect of taxol binding, which also promotes an expanded conformation of αβ-tubulin in a GDP lattice (Alushin et al., 2014).
evidence: Comparison to cited structural study of taxol effects

claim: The β:T238A mutation substantially uncouples the conformational cycle from the nucleotide cycle in the lattice.
source: Simply put, the mutation appears to have substantially uncoupled the conformational cycle from the nucleotide cycle in the lattice, allowing αβ-tubulin to retain GTP-lattice-like character even in a GDP lattice.
evidence: Concluded from Bim1 binding showing GTP-like conformation despite GDP nucleotide

claim: EB1 proteins do not bind at the very microtubule end.
source: The Bim1 experiments described above do not report on the conformation of αβ-tubulin at the very microtubule end because EB1 proteins do not bind there (Maurer et al., 2012; 2014).
evidence: Cited from prior studies of EB1 binding

claim: Isolated TOG domains from Stu2p stimulate the depolymerization of stabilized microtubules in a dose-dependent way.
source: After fortuitously discovering that isolated TOG domains from the microtubule polymerase Stu2p stimulate the depolymerization of stabilized microtubules in a dose-dependent way
evidence: Observed experimentally

claim: The underlying cause of TOG-induced depolymerization is TOG-mediated stabilization of the curved and faster dissociating conformation of αβ-tubulin on the microtubule end.
source: we reasoned that the underlying cause of this induced depolymerization was TOG-mediated stabilization of the curved and faster dissociating conformation of αβ-tubulin on the microtubule end (Figure 5).
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on TOG binding preferences

claim: The rate of TOG-induced depolymerization increases linearly over at least a 20-fold range of TOG concentration.
source: Using drug-stabilized microtubules as a substrate, the rate of TOG-induced depolymerization increases linearly over at least a 20-fold range of TOG concentration.
evidence: Measured in depolymerization assays shown in Figure 5B

claim: The linear concentration-dependence of TOG-induced depolymerization is consistent with a collisional mechanism in which the rate-limiting step is a TOG domain arriving at the microtubule end.
source: This linear concentration-dependence is consistent with a collisional mechanism in which the rate-limiting step is a TOG domain arriving at the microtubule end.
evidence: Inferred from the linear dose-response relationship

claim: Drug-stabilized β:T238A microtubules depolymerize substantially slower than wild-type at the same concentration of TOG domain.
source: Drug-stabilized β:T238A microtubules depolymerize substantially slower than wild-type at the same concentration of TOG domain (Figure 5).
evidence: Measured in depolymerization assays shown in Figure 5

claim: Only at higher TOG concentrations do β:T238A microtubules show appreciable dose-dependent TOG-induced depolymerization.
source: Only at higher TOG concentrations do β:T238A microtubules show appreciable dose-dependent TOG-induced depolymerization (Figure 5).
evidence: Shown in depolymerization assays in Figure 5B inset

claim: Similar TOG-induced depolymerization results were obtained using MTs stabilized with GTPγS.
source: Similar results were obtained using MTs stabilized with GTPγS (Figure 5).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5B

claim: TOG domains bind with comparable affinity to curved wild-type and mutant αβ-tubulin.
source: TOG domains bind with comparable affinity to curved wild-type and mutant αβ-tubulin, so differences in TOG affinity cannot explain the markedly slower TOG-induced shrinking of β:T238A microtubules.
evidence: Established from earlier TOG binding experiments (Figure 3B)

claim: A mutant-induced change in the propensity to become/remain straight on the microtubule end is the simplest way to explain both the slower post-catastrophe shrinking and weaker TOG-induced depolymerization for the mutant.
source: Thus, a mutant-induced change in the propensity to become/remain straight on the microtubule end is the simplest way to explain both the slower post-catastrophe shrinking and weaker TOG-induced depolymerization for the mutant.
evidence: Concluded from integrating TOG binding and depolymerization data

claim: The conformation of end-bound αβ-tubulins is affected by the β:T238A mutation.
source: That the conformation of end-bound αβ-tubulins is affected by the β:T238A mutation is also consistent with the Bim1 coating, which demonstrated that the mutation affected αβ-tubulin conformation elsewhere in the lattice.
evidence: Inferred from TOG-induced depolymerization and Bim1 coating data

claim: Yeast expressing β:T238S αβ-tubulin are comparably benomyl resistant to β:T238A.
source: Yeast expressing β:T238S αβ-tubulin are comparably benomyl resistant to β:T238A, but significantly less benomyl dependent (Figure 6A).
evidence: Shown in growth assays in Figure 6A

claim: Yeast expressing β:T238V αβ-tubulin are substantially less resistant to benomyl than β:T238A, and show no benomyl dependence.
source: By contrast, yeast expressing β:T238V αβ-tubulin are substantially less resistant to benomyl, and show no benomyl dependence (Figure 6A).
evidence: Shown in growth assays in Figure 6A

claim: β:T238S microtubules are β:T238A-like (static) in vivo.
source: Measurements of microtubule dynamics in vivo are consistent with the benomyl phenotypes: β:T238S microtubules are β:T238A-like (static) whereas β:T238V microtubules are more wild-type-like (dynamic but with somewhat slower shrinking) (Figure 6B).
evidence: Measured by in vivo imaging shown in Figure 6B

claim: β:T238V microtubules are more wild-type-like (dynamic but with somewhat slower shrinking) in vivo.
source: Measurements of microtubule dynamics in vivo are consistent with the benomyl phenotypes: β:T238S microtubules are β:T238A-like (static) whereas β:T238V microtubules are more wild-type-like (dynamic but with somewhat slower shrinking) (Figure 6B).
evidence: Measured by in vivo imaging shown in Figure 6B

claim: The trend with sidechain size and the strong effect obtained from the Thr to Ser mutation at position 238 suggest that some form of 'steric overpacking', not hydrogen bonding, contributes to destabilize the straight, expanded conformation of αβ-tubulin in microtubules containing GDP.
source: The trend with sidechain size and the strong effect obtained from the Thr to Ser mutation at position 238 suggest that some form of 'steric overpacking', not hydrogen bonding, contributes to destabilize the straight, expanded conformation of αβ-tubulin in microtubules containing GDP.
evidence: Inferred from comparing phenotypes of different substitutions at position 238

claim: β:C354A or β:C354S substitutions dramatically reduced the rate of microtubule shrinking and the frequency of catastrophe.
source: Indeed, β:C354A or β:C354S substitutions dramatically reduced the rate of microtubule shrinking and the frequency of catastrophe (Gupta et al., 2002).
evidence: Cited from prior study

claim: β:C354A microtubules show Bim1-GFP coating similar to β:T238A.
source: β:C354A microtubules showed Bim1-GFP coating similar to what we observed for β:T238A, indicating the two mutations stabilize microtubules through a common conformational mechanism (Figure 6C).
evidence: Shown in Bim1-GFP binding experiments in Figure 6C

claim: The β:T238A and β:C354A mutations stabilize microtubules through a common conformational mechanism.
source: β:C354A microtubules showed Bim1-GFP coating similar to what we observed for β:T238A, indicating the two mutations stabilize microtubules through a common conformational mechanism (Figure 6C).
evidence: Inferred from similar Bim1-GFP binding patterns

claim: Positions 238 and 354 in β-tubulin show strong evolutionary conservation (β:238 is 65% T and 34% C whereas β:354 is 99% C).
source: Positions 238 and 354 in β-tubulin show strong evolutionarily conservation (yeast numbering; β:238 is 65% T and 34% C whereas β:354 is 99% C), consistent with an important functional role for these residues.
evidence: Determined from sequence conservation analysis

claim: Changes in packing volume near helix H7 can dictate the dynamic properties of microtubules by tuning an allosteric response to GDP.
source: Together, the β:T238A and β:C354A results suggest that changes in packing volume near helix H7 can dictate the dynamic properties of microtubules by tuning an allosteric response to GDP.
evidence: Concluded from comparing effects of mutations at positions 238 and 354

claim: Relatively conservative buried mutations in β-tubulin can diminish the conformational response to GDP in the lattice.
source: We demonstrate that relatively conservative buried mutations in β-tubulin can diminish the conformational response to GDP in the lattice, and that this altered structural response yields dramatic effects on microtubule dynamics.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: Mutations can uncouple the conformational and nucleotide cycles of αβ-tubulin.
source: By discovering that mutations can uncouple the conformational and nucleotide cycles of αβ-tubulin, our findings provide new insights into ways that the αβ-tubulin conformational cycle dictates microtubule polymerization dynamics (Figure 7).
evidence: Demonstrated through multiple experiments showing GTP-like conformation with GDP nucleotide

claim: In the lattice, a major effect of the β:T238A mutation is to substantially suppress conformational changes that normally occur as a consequence of GTPase activity.
source: Our experiments using the EB1 family protein Bim1 showed that in the lattice a major effect of the β:T238A mutation is to substantially suppress conformational changes that normally occur as a consequence of GTPase activity (Hyman et al., 1995; Alushin et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: Demonstrated by Bim1 binding experiments showing GTP-like binding to GDP lattice

claim: The mutant microtubule lattice retains more GTP-like character than wild-type.
source: However, the stronger binding of Bim1 to GDP-containing β:T238A microtubules indicates that the mutant microtubule lattice retains more GTP-like character than does wild-type.
evidence: Inferred from Bim1 binding data

claim: The slow shrinking and lower frequency of catastrophe in the mutant most likely result from the attenuated allosteric response to GDP.
source: Thus, the slow shrinking and lower frequency of catastrophe in the mutant most likely result from the attenuated allosteric response to GDP; this in turn results in a straighter and more strongly associated GTP-like conformation on the microtubule end, despite having GDP at the longitudinal interface (Figure 7B).
evidence: Concluded from integrating structural and dynamic data

claim: The majority of the mutation-induced effects are confined to post-GTPase conformational changes in the lattice.
source: It is remarkable that the majority of the mutation-induced effects are confined to post-GTPase conformational changes in the lattice.
evidence: Observed from the pattern of effects across different assays

claim: Not observing significant effects on elongation is somewhat surprising, because it had been anticipated that the conformational changes required to enter the lattice would contribute to polymerization dynamics by opposing incorporation into the lattice.
source: Not observing significant effects on elongation is somewhat surprising, because it had been anticipated that the conformational changes required to enter the lattice would contribute to polymerization dynamics by opposing incorporation into the lattice.
evidence: Discussion of expectations versus observations

claim: The increased spontaneous nucleation of β:T238A αβ-tubulin in the presence of GTPγS indicates that the mutation affects conformational transitions that occur in/on a GTP lattice.
source: However, this is not consistent with increased spontaneous nucleation of β:T238A αβ-tubulin in the presence of GTPγS, which indicated that the mutation did affect conformational transitions that occur in/on a GTP lattice.
evidence: Observed in nucleation experiments with GTPγS

claim: The energetics of curved to straight transitions on the microtubule end may not be rate-contributing for elongation, perhaps because these transitions occur subsequent to end binding.
source: It could be that we did not observe substantial effects on elongation because the energetics of curved to straight transitions on the microtubule end are not rate-contributing for elongation, perhaps because these transitions occur subsequent to end binding.
evidence: Proposed explanation for lack of elongation effects

claim: The differential response to the mutation inside and outside of microtubules is consistent with the view that the curved conformation represents the 'ground state' of αβ-tubulin independent of nucleotide state.
source: The differential response to the mutation inside and outside of microtubules (Figure 7A,B) is consistent with the view that the curved conformation represents the 'ground state' of αβ-tubulin independent of nucleotide state (Rice et al., 2008; Buey et al., 2006; Nawrotek et al., 2011; Pecqueur et al., 2012; Ayaz et al., 2012)
evidence: Interpretation supported by cited prior work

claim: The nucleotide acts across the longitudinal interface.
source: The differential response to the mutation inside and outside of microtubules (Figure 7A,B) is consistent with the view that the curved conformation represents the 'ground state' of αβ-tubulin independent of nucleotide state (Rice et al., 2008; Buey et al., 2006; Nawrotek et al., 2011; Pecqueur et al., 2012; Ayaz et al., 2012), that the nucleotide acts across the longitudinal interface (Rice et al., 2008; Nawrotek et al., 2011)
evidence: Interpretation supported by cited prior work

claim: Nucleotide-dependent interactions with the microtubule lattice are what drive αβ-tubulin conformational transitions.
source: that nucleotide-dependent interactions with the microtubule lattice are what drive αβ-tubulin conformational transitions (Rice et al., 2008; Buey et al., 2006; Nawrotek et al., 2011).
evidence: Interpretation supported by cited prior work and current data

claim: The changes observed can largely be explained by an impaired allosteric response to GDP in the lattice.
source: Indeed, the changes we observed can largely be explained by an impaired allosteric response to GDP in the lattice.
evidence: Summary interpretation of all experimental findings

claim: Buried mutations of or near β:T238 alter the allosteric response to GDP in the microtubule lattice, with dramatic consequences for catastrophe frequency and shrinking rate.
source: In summary, we showed that buried mutations of or near β:T238 alter the allosteric response to GDP in the microtubule lattice, with dramatic consequences for catastrophe frequency and shrinking rate.
evidence: Summary of main findings

claim: Allostery in the lattice dictates functionally important aspects of microtubule polymerization dynamics.
source: By describing microtubules with identical interface composition that nevertheless undergo strikingly different polymerization dynamics, our data demonstrate that allostery in the lattice dictates functionally important aspects of microtubule polymerization dynamics (Figure 7C).
evidence: Concluded from comparing wild-type and mutant microtubules with same nucleotide but different dynamics

claim: Cooperative conformational linkage in the lattice amplifies the individual response to nucleotide.
source: Based on the central role of allostery in controlling the frequency of catastrophe and the rate of shrinking, we speculate that cooperative conformational linkage in the lattice amplifies the individual response to nucleotide.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the role of allostery

claim: The allosteric response to GDP and the intrinsic bias of αβ-tubulin toward the curved conformation elevate and separate the threshold concentrations for persistent elongation and for spontaneous nucleation.
source: Together, the allosteric response to GDP and the intrinsic bias of αβ-tubulin toward the curved conformation elevate and separate the threshold concentrations for persistent elongation and for spontaneous nucleation (Figure 7C)
evidence: Concluded from comparing wild-type and mutant behavior

claim: The allosteric response to GDP and intrinsic curvature bias underlie the fast shrinking rate that makes catastrophe more decisive.
source: Together, the allosteric response to GDP and the intrinsic bias of αβ-tubulin toward the curved conformation elevate and separate the threshold concentrations for persistent elongation and for spontaneous nucleation (Figure 7C), and underlie the fast shrinking rate that makes catastrophe more decisive.
evidence: Concluded from comparing wild-type and mutant shrinking rates

claim: Allosteric contributions to microtubule dynamics make microtubules more amenable to regulation by cellular factors that enhance elongation, trigger catastrophe, and promote nucleation.
source: These allosteric contributions to microtubule dynamics make microtubules more amenable to regulation by cellular factors that enhance elongation, trigger catastrophe, and promote nucleation.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the functional significance of allostery

claim: Helix H7 is positioned differently in the 'curved' (unpolymerized) and 'straight' (polymerized) conformations of αβ-tubulin.
source: We focused on helix H7 because it is an element that is positioned differently in the 'curved' (unpolymerized) and 'straight' (polymerized) conformations of αβ-tubulin (Nogales et al., 1998; Ravelli et al., 2004)(Figure 1A)
evidence: Cited from structural studies and shown in Figure 1A

claim: Helix H7 may act as a structural relay connecting the 'top' and 'bottom' of the tubulin subunits.
source: it may act as a structural relay connecting the 'top' and 'bottom' of the tubulin subunits (Amos, 2004).
evidence: Cited from prior structural analysis

claim: The equivalent helix in α-tubulin was recently observed to move in response to GTP hydrolysis in the lattice.
source: The equivalent helix in α-tubulin was also recently observed to move in response to GTP hydrolysis in the lattice (Alushin et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from recent cryo-EM study

claim: Prior studies showed that the β:T238A phenotype was consistent with hyperstable microtubules.
source: because prior studies (Thomas et al., 1985; Machin et al., 1995) showed that the β:T238A phenotype was consistent with hyperstable microtubules.
evidence: Cited from prior genetic studies

claim: The molecular mechanism by which the β:T238A mutation affects microtubule dynamics was unknown prior to this study.
source: The molecular mechanism by which the β:T238A mutation affects microtubule dynamics is unknown, in part because the polymerization dynamics of β:T238A αβ-tubulin have not been studied in vivo or in vitro.
evidence: Statement of knowledge gap

claim: The β:T238A mutation affects microtubule dynamics by dramatically reducing the frequency of catastrophe and the rate of shrinking.
source: Our studies now reveal that the β:T238A mutation affects microtubule dynamics by dramatically reducing the frequency of catastrophe and the rate of shrinking
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: The β:T238A mutation affects microtubule structure by attenuating post-GTPase conformational changes in the lattice.
source: the mutation affects microtubule structure by attenuating post-GTPase conformational changes in the lattice.
evidence: Summary of structural findings from Bim1 experiments

claim: The β:T238A mutation weakens the coupling between the conformational and GTPase cycles of αβ-tubulin.
source: By showing that the β:T238A mutation weakens the coupling between the conformational and nucleotide cycles
evidence: Summary interpretation of findings

claim: Catastrophe can occur despite diminished post-GTPase conformational changes in the microtubule lattice.
source: our results demonstrate that catastrophe can occur despite diminished post-GTPase conformational changes in the microtubule lattice
evidence: Demonstrated by observing catastrophe in mutant microtubules with attenuated conformational response

claim: The strength of the allosteric response to GDP dictates the rate of microtubule shrinking and the frequency of microtubule catastrophe.
source: the strength of the allosteric response to GDP dictates the rate of microtubule shrinking and the frequency of microtubule catastrophe.
evidence: Concluded from comparing wild-type and mutant with different allosteric responses

claim: Microtubule dynamic instability depends on the GTPase activity of the polymerizing αβ-tubulin subunits.
source: Microtubule dynamic instability depends on the GTPase activity of the polymerizing αβ-tubulin subunits, which cycle through at least three distinct conformations as they move into and out of microtubules.
evidence: Established knowledge in the field

claim: αβ-tubulin cycles through at least three distinct conformations as they move into and out of microtubules.
source: Microtubule dynamic instability depends on the GTPase activity of the polymerizing αβ-tubulin subunits, which cycle through at least three distinct conformations as they move into and out of microtubules.
evidence: Established knowledge from structural studies

claim: Unpolymerized αβ-tubulin adopts a 'curved' conformation.
source: Unpolymerized αβ-tubulin adopts a 'curved' conformation (Ravelli et al., 2004; Rice et al., 2008; Buey et al., 2006) that is not compatible with the 'straight' microtubule lattice (Nogales et al., 1998).
evidence: Cited from structural studies

claim: The curved conformation of unpolymerized αβ-tubulin is not compatible with the 'straight' microtubule lattice.
source: Unpolymerized αβ-tubulin adopts a 'curved' conformation (Ravelli et al., 2004; Rice et al., 2008; Buey et al., 2006) that is not compatible with the 'straight' microtubule lattice (Nogales et al., 1998).
evidence: Cited from structural studies

claim: In the body of the microtubule, αβ-tubulin can adopt distinct 'expanded' or 'compacted' straight conformations depending on nucleotide state.
source: In the body of the microtubule, αβ-tubulin can adopt distinct 'expanded' or 'compacted' straight conformations depending on nucleotide state (Alushin et al., 2014; Hyman et al., 1995).
evidence: Cited from structural and biochemical studies

claim: EB1 family proteins mark the plus-end cap of microtubules by binding preferentially to the 'expanded', GTP-like conformation of αβ-tubulin.
source: In one well-characterized example, end-binding proteins in the EB1 family have been shown to mark the plus-end cap of microtubules by binding preferentially to the 'expanded', GTP-like conformation of αβ-tubulin that only occurs near the end of the growing microtubule lattice (Maurer et al., 2011; 2012; Zanic et al., 2009; Alushin et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from prior studies of EB1 proteins

claim: TOG domains from Stu2p bind preferentially to the curved conformation of αβ-tubulin.
source: Another recent example of selective interactions with specific conformations of αβ-tubulin comes from work in our laboratory showing that TOG domains from the microtubule polymerase Stu2p bind preferentially to the curved conformation of αβ-tubulin (Ayaz et al., 2012; 2014)
evidence: Cited from prior work from the authors' laboratory

claim: The preference of TOG domains for curved αβ-tubulin is probably what allows the polymerase to localize to the growing tip of the microtubule.
source: this preference of TOG domains for curved αβ-tubulin is probably what allows the polymerase to localize to the growing tip of the microtubule (Ayaz et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from prior work with mechanistic interpretation

claim: Selective binding to distinct conformations of αβ-tubulin represents a common and important strategy for recognizing and controlling microtubules.
source: These and numerous studies of other regulatory proteins (Desai et al., 1999; Gigant et al., 2000; Peters et al., 2010; Alushin et al., 2010; Bechstedt et al., 2014) contribute to the emerging view that selective binding to distinct conformations of αβ-tubulin represents a common and important strategy for recognizing and controlling microtubules.
evidence: Synthesis of multiple cited studies

claim: How the αβ-tubulin conformational cycle contributes to microtubule dynamics is less understood.
source: How the αβ-tubulin conformational cycle contributes to microtubule dynamics is less understood.
evidence: Statement of knowledge gap in the field

claim: Showing that conformational rearrangements in αβ-tubulin contribute to and are required for the dynamic properties of microtubules remains challenging.
source: Indeed, even though structural rearrangements in αβ-tubulin have long been known to occur during and after microtubule incorporation (Mandelkow et al., 1991b; Chrétien et al., 1995; Hyman et al., 1995), actually showing that these rearrangements contribute to and are required for the dynamic properties of microtubules remains challenging (Rice et al., 2008; Wang and Nogales, 2005; Buey et al., 2006; Jánosi et al., 2002; Molodtsov et al., 2005).
evidence: Statement of ongoing challenge in the field with citations

claim: To date, in vitro microtubule dynamics have only been measured for a small number of αβ-tubulin mutants.
source: One reason these questions are still debated is that to date in vitro microtubule dynamics have only been measured for a small number of αβ-tubulin mutants (Gupta et al., 2002; Dougherty et al., 2001; Sage et al., 1995)
evidence: Statement of limitation in the field with citations

claim: It has not yet been possible to link altered dynamics to a change in the αβ-tubulin conformational cycle.
source: it has not yet been possible to link altered dynamics to a change in the αβ-tubulin conformational cycle.
evidence: Statement of knowledge gap

claim: GTP-bound αβ-tubulin 'straightens' during the formation of longitudinal and lateral lattice contacts.
source: For example, GTP-bound αβ-tubulin 'straightens' during the formation of longitudinal and lateral lattice contacts (Buey et al., 2006; Rice et al., 2008; Nawrotek et al., 2011)
evidence: Cited from prior structural studies

claim: β:T238A microtubules were on average over 50% longer than wild-type microtubules in yeast cells.
source: These measurements revealed that β:T238A-tubulin forms static microtubules (neither growing nor shrinking) that are on average over 50% longer than the dynamic microtubules that form in a strain with wild-type β-tubulin (Figure 1B and Videos 1,2).
evidence: Measured from in vivo imaging data in Figure 1B

claim: β:T238A-tubulin forms static microtubules (neither growing nor shrinking) in yeast cells.
source: These measurements revealed that β:T238A-tubulin forms static microtubules (neither growing nor shrinking) that are on average over 50% longer than the dynamic microtubules that form in a strain with wild-type β-tubulin (Figure 1B and Videos 1,2).
evidence: Observed in time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 1B and Videos 1,2

claim: The striking change in microtubule dynamics caused by β:T238A cannot be the result of a direct perturbation of a polymerization interface or of an interaction with regulatory proteins.
source: Because the mutated site is solvent inaccessible, this striking change in microtubule dynamics cannot be the result of a direct perturbation of a polymerization interface or of an interaction with one or more regulatory proteins.
evidence: Inferred from the buried nature of the mutation site

claim: Wild-type and β:T238A αβ-tubulin could not be measured at equivalent concentrations in dynamics assays.
source: We were unable to measure mutant and wild-type microtubule dynamics at equivalent concentrations, because β:T238A αβ-tubulin showed abundant spontaneous nucleation at the higher concentrations where we measured wild-type, and wild-type αβ-tubulin does not elongate measurably at the low concentrations where we were able to measure β:T238A dynamics without excessive nucleation.
evidence: Experimental observation and limitation

claim: The x-intercept and slope of elongation rate plots respectively relate to the apparent affinity and association rate constant for elongation.
source: Because the x-intercept and slope respectively relate to the apparent affinity and association rate constant for elongation, our data indicate that the mutation has little effect on the apparent biochemistry of microtubule elongation.
evidence: Standard interpretation of kinetic parameters

claim: The β:T238A mutation has little effect on the apparent biochemistry of microtubule elongation.
source: Because the x-intercept and slope respectively relate to the apparent affinity and association rate constant for elongation, our data indicate that the mutation has little effect on the apparent biochemistry of microtubule elongation.
evidence: Inferred from similar slopes of elongation rate plots

claim: The lower catastrophe frequency of β:T238A is especially notable considering that the mutant microtubules were growing much slower than wild-type due to lower tubulin concentration.
source: The lower catastrophe frequency we observed is especially notable when considering that in these assays the T238A microtubules were growing much slower than wild-type because of the ∼threefold lower concentration of αβ-tubulin used for the mutant (Figure 1E, top).
evidence: Observation from comparing experimental conditions

claim: Yeast microtubules have previously been reported to contain more GTP than vertebrate microtubules.
source: Yeast microtubules have previously been reported to contain more GTP than vertebrate microtubules (Dougherty et al., 1998).
evidence: Cited from prior study

claim: In control experiments, vertebrate microtubules contain very little GTP.
source: In control experiments (not shown) we confirmed that vertebrate microtubules contain very little GTP and that individual heterodimers were not pelleting.
evidence: Performed as control experiments

claim: It seems unlikely that wild-type yeast microtubules contain substantial amounts of GTP based on fast shrinking, little 32P-GTP in GTPγS microtubules, and normal EB1 recognition.
source: Because we observed very fast shrinking (Figure 1), little 32P-GTP in microtubules grown with GTPγS (Figure 2C), and normal plus-end recognition by an EB1 family protein (see below), it seems unlikely that wild-type yeast microtubules contain substantial amounts of GTP.
evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of evidence
